title: Falafel
wiki_lead:
Falafel ( fə-LAH-fəl; Arabic: فلافل, IPA: [fæˈlæːfɪl] ) is a deep-fried ball or patty-shaped fritter of Egyptian origin that features in Middle Eastern cuisine, particularly Levantine cuisines. It is made from ground fava beans, chickpeas, or both, and mixed with herbs and spices before frying.
Falafel is often served in a flatbread such as pita, samoon, laffa, or taboon; falafel also frequently refers to a wrapped sandwich that is prepared in this way. The falafel balls may be topped with salads, pickled vegetables, and hot sauce, and drizzled with tahini-based sauces. Falafel balls may also be eaten alone as a snack or served as part of a meze tray.
Falafel is a popular street food eaten throughout the Middle East. In Egypt and the Arabian Peninsula, it is most often made with fava beans, while in the Levant, it is typically made with chickpeas or sometimes a blend of both.
Falafel has been the subject of gastronationalistic campaigns in many Middle Eastern countries, most notably in the Israeli–Palestinian conflict, where both sides have claimed ownership of the dish.

Etymology
The word falāfil (Arabic: فلافل) is Arabic and is the plural of filfil (فلفل) 'pepper', borrowed from Persian felfel (فلفل), cognate with the Sanskrit word pippalī (पिप्पली) 'long pepper'; or an earlier *filfal, from Aramaic pilpāl 'small round thing, peppercorn', derived from palpēl 'to be round, roll'.
The name falāfil is used world-wide. In English (where it has been written falafel, felafel, filafel and filafil), it is first attested in 1936.
Falafel is known as ṭaʿmiyya (Arabic: طعمية, IPA: [tˤɑʕˈmejjɑ]) in Egypt and Sudan. The word is derived from a diminutive form of the Arabic word ṭaʿām (طعام, 'food'); the particular form indicates a "unit" of the given root in this case Ṭ-ʕ-M (ط ع م, having to do with taste and food), thus meaning 'a little piece of food' or 'small tasty thing'.
The word falafel can refer to the fritters themselves or to sandwiches filled with them.


History and distribution

The origin of falafel is uncertain. The dish most likely originated in Egypt. It has been speculated that its history may go back to Pharaonic Egypt. However, the earliest written references to falafel from Egyptian sources date to the 19th century, and oil was probably too expensive to use for deep frying in ancient Egypt. Another theory regarding the origins of falafel is that the dish was created when British soldiers from India, craving Indian cuisine, began making or having made replacements for Indian cuisine in Egypt. This theory is supported by circumstantial evidence though no conclusive evidence for it exists.

As Alexandria is a port city, it was possible to export the dish and its name to other areas in the Middle East. It first spread south into the rest of Egypt, but after World War 1 it began to spread outside of Egypt. grok_lead: Falafel is a deep-fried fritter typically formed into balls or patties from ground chickpeas, fava beans, or a mixture of both, blended with herbs such as parsley and cilantro, onions, garlic, and spices including cumin and coriander. The dish most likely originated in Egypt, where it is known as ta'ameya and traditionally made with fava beans. A frequently cited theory attributes it to Coptic Christians as a Lenten meat substitute, though this lacks strong primary-source support. It later became a staple street food across the Middle East, particularly in Levantine countries such as Lebanon, Syria, Palestine, and Israel, where chickpea-based versions predominate. Commonly served in pita bread with tahini sauce, chopped vegetables, and pickles, falafel provides a protein-rich, vegetarian option that has gained global popularity, though disputes persist over its cultural ownership amid broader gastronationalist tensions in the region. Traditional preparation involves soaking dried legumes overnight, processing into a coarse mixture without cooking them prior to frying to achieve a crispy exterior and fluffy interior, distinguishing authentic recipes from those using canned beans which yield denser results.
